doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Stage presence and presenting jazz: Clark Terry, Flip Phillips
summary: Warmth like Clark Terry's and accessible originals like Flip Phillips's 'The Claw' win audiences; she dislikes suffering-artist seriousness.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well you know jazz I think takes some work to listen to. I think it’s not as easily accessible to peoples’ ears somehow. A lot of people don’t understand — oh I like jazz
until they stop playing the melody. They don’t quite know how to listen to it and I’m not sure that they really should.

It also boils down to the way that it’s presented also. And the artist. Like someone who I idolize with their stage presence and something I always try to learn from people who are great band leaders and understand what — I mean you can warm up to somebody really fast, you can really like someone even if you’re not a hundred percent convinced you like the music they’re playing. Like Clark [Terry] is so open and so warm and he’s just so, it’s like he just walks out and gives the audience a big hug or something. And he does a lot of original tunes, but they’re sort of stylized so people will like be comfortable with the feel his group plays with. They don’t play anything crazy or play free or sound like the drums are falling down a flight of stairs or anything. But he does a lot of original music. And Flip Phillips, who was here last year, who just played so great, played a lot of original stuff, music he wrote on “Sweet Georgia Brown,” on those chord changes. We play one of his songs based on “I Got Rhythm,” that’s called “The Claw.” We played it yesterday and the audience loved it but they don’t know that song. They could never sing that song. That song has a really fast bebop head that would be like alien to an audience like this. But it was Flip Phillips and it’s straight ahead swing, and maybe they recognized the “I Got Rhythm” chord changes, I don’t know. But there’s ways to do it and to present it and find a combination that doesn’t make it so difficult. And if you have — a lot of jazz musicians are, you know, my friends used to say “yeah isn’t it weird, jazz musicians think jazz is an open wound let’s pour salt in it, we just have to suffer, and be all like suffering for our art because this is the blues.” And it’s like uh huh. Hey all right. I don’t think so. And they look so serious. And a lot of artists are so introverted and so like just into their art, I’m an artist, I’m going to be as weird as possible and alienate you and turn my back to you. You know and it’s like no, it’s not fun. I like to have fun when I play, and I always do. And I think the audience reacts to that also, rather than they get scared if you’re all serious and dark and crazy acting, and they’re like, “ooh, what are we listening to?” I mean you could play “Take the A Train” with a weird attitude and scare people too.
I love it when people do creative things, even with someone last night was doing—
“Sunny Side of the Street.” And they were playing it in two keys.
Yeah. C and E flat. Yeah.

And I couldn’t figure out what was going on for a minute. I thought I knew what song this was and then it shifted and I’m going that was really neat. Wasn’t your tenor player playing in that set I think?
